messages.subject: [statnet_help] addition of NA in $mel after simulate.ergm
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] addition of NA in $mel after simulate.ergm
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have a question regarding the simulate.ergm. For example

[R code]
require(ergm)
data(florentine)
length(flomarriage$mel) # 20
network.edgecount(flomarriage) #20

gest <- ergm(flomarriage ~ edges + absdiff("wealth"))

set.seed(2013)
ssim <- simulate(gest)

length(ssim$mel) #45
network.edgecount(ssim) #25

[/R code]

The discrepancy between length(ssim$mel) and network.edgecount(ssim)
can be explored by closer look at the ssim$mel. Twenty NA edges were
added and thus the eids are inflated by 20, the original edge count in
flomarriage.
It is reproducible in another dataset such as samplike

[R code]
require(ergm)
data("sampson")
set.seed(2013)
simulate(ergm(samplike~edges))$mel
[/R code]

88 NA edges were added this time.

I would like to know the reason for addition of NA edges. Are these NA
edges functional?

Thank you!

Regards,

CH

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Help with ergm
messages.body_plain:
Dear Statnet users and developers,

I'm using the statnet package for PhD work, and first I'd like to thank 
the developers for creating such wonderful tools. However I have a few 
problems with my ERGMs that I couldn't resolve with the documentation, 
and I was hoping you could help.

I'm working with a new dataset that we collected with a Facebook app 
that works as a survey (https://sns.it.helsinki.fi). So far we have a 
fairly large dataset of Facebook friendships and survey answers for the 
vertices (6000 vertices and 25000 edges).

I'm using the ergm package to estimate a model very similar to the one 
used by Wimmer & Lewis (2010) in their brilliant paper in American 
Journal of Sociology. My biggest problem, I think, is getting converged 
MCMC samples out of the model.

In verbose mode ergm outputs some statistics labelled "Back from 
unconstrained MCMC. Average statistics:". I couldn't find documentation 
on what they mean, but have I guessed correctly that they equal the MCMC 
sample average of the count statistics minus the observed count 
statistics? The mcmc.diagnostics function indicates that they differ 
significantly from zero, which I understand means poor convergence of 
the MCMC (or poor fit of the model)?

I guess I need really long MCMC runs, but I feel that the MCMC algorithm 
seems to slow down the further it goes. I observe this especially with 
verbose mode when I use short burnins with many retries: Each retry 
seems to take longer to compute than the previous. Is this something 
that should happen or can it be avoided somehow? And for many 
configurations, the process seems to freeze completely at some point. 
The last output says "Burn-in failed to converge or mixed..."

Also I noticed that you added support for parallel computing. Has anyone 
tried to run ergm massively parallel with MPI? I have access to 
computers where I could run it with a few hundred cores and I was 
wondering would it be worth the effort.

For further details I attached one of my outputs, where I chose 
parameters so that the script finishes. I've been using ergm versions 
3.0-3 and 3.0-999. I would be really grateful for any tips on getting 
better results with the model.

Yours sincerely,
Juha Itkonen

messages.body_plain:
Dear User community,

I am now analyzing bipartite graphs, ran the model, and ran simulations for goodness of fit in terms of degrees and geodesics distance.

My model includes 165(b1) + 150 (b2)=250 nodes, and 701 edges. My model also includes: exogenous var+gwb1dgree+gwb2degree+wgdsp.
>mygof<-gof(mynet<-degree+distance, burnin=1e+5, interval=1e+5, seed=100)

My model predict a good degree distribution, however diminum geodesics was dissapointint.  It is very similar picture of 
David R. Hunter, Steven M. Goodreau, and Mark S. Handcock, "Goodness of fit of social network models," American Ststistical Association Journal, 2008, Vol 103, No. 481, p. 256, Figure 4, right-hand column.

Their geodesic distance problem was improved, after they had included GWEPS statistics.  But, GWESP (edge-wise SP) does not make sense for bipartite.

If anyone knows how to improve Bipartite geodesics goodness of fit, please reply here.  Or, is the problem of over-predict the short distances and under-predict the longer distance often a problem for bipartites??, because there is no triangular relations, as actors are connected to other actors through edges by definition??

I appreciate your reply in advance.

Best regards,

Megumi Nishimura
Faculty of Law
Ritsumeikan University

messages.body_plain:
Dear user community,

I am interested in the homophily effects in bipartite networks. 

Please ask the community if I am running the correct model, and other multicollenearity questions.

We examine if the citizen donate money to their own professional organizations. And, I will run ERGM model WITH keeping bipartite structure.

I would like to know if people donate money to their own professional organization

Assume I code the doctors as 1, farmers as 2, and managers as 3.  Then, I code the doctor's organization as 1, farmer's organization as 2, manager's Organization as 3.  I have 10 actors (b1), 5 organization (events, b2).  Edges are non-valued, and non-directed.

I make a bipartite R network object, called "mynet."
attached the following combined ethnic variable to "mynet."
combeth<-c(1, 3, 2, 2, 3, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 1, 3, 2, 1, 1)
mynet<-set.vertex.attribute(mynet, "combinedethnic", combeth)

Then, run an ergm model with nodematch command,
mymodel1<-ergm(mynet~edges+nodematch("combinedethnic", diff=T, keep=c(1, 2, 3))+wg1bdegree(0.25), seed=100)

QUESTION1) I got an output, but would like to know nodematch is a right command to analyze my research question above for BIPARTITE??

QUESTION 2) If I recode the ethnic variable into like the following, and is included in my model, do we have multicollinearity problem?
Men lawyers as 1, Women lawyers as 2, Men farmers as 3, Women farmers as 4, Men managers as 5. Women managers as 6. Make a ethnic variable
geneth<-c(1, 3, 5, 2, 4, 5, 3, 2, 1, 3, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA)

Then, run ergm,
mymodel2<-ergm(mynet~edges+bafactor(geneth, base=1)+nodematch("combinedethnic", diff=T, keep=c(1, 2, 3))+gwb1degree(0.25), seed=100)

Q2) Do we have a multicollenearity problem, because our "combinedethnic" and "geneth" variables are so similar?

Q3) Finally, if we have multicollinearity problem, how do we detect it.  Does the model simply clash? or show degeneracy? or bad p-values on the difference between sample statistics and the observed one? or other statistics?

I appreciate your replies in advance.

Best regards,

Megumi Nishimura
Faculty of Law
Ritsumeikan University

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] re: goodness of fit in geodesic for bipartite
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
> My model predict a good degree distribution, however diminum geodesics was dissapointint.  It is very similar picture of 
> David R. Hunter, Steven M. Goodreau, and Mark S. Handcock, "Goodness of fit of social network models," American Ststistical Association Journal, 2008, Vol 103, No. 481, p. 256, Figure 4, right-hand column.
>
> Their geodesic distance problem was improved, after they had included GWEPS statistics.  But, GWESP (edge-wise SP) does not make sense for bipartite.
>
> If anyone knows how to improve Bipartite geodesics goodness of fit, please reply here.  Or, is the problem of over-predict the short distances and under-predict the longer distance often a problem for bipartites??, because there is no triangular relations, as actors are connected to other actors through edges by definition??

I do not work with bipartite affillation-style networks myself, but I
have a feeling that this pattern is quite common across many kinds of
networks. As long as there are some forms of clustering that is strong
but not complete (ie with some ties between clusters) occurring that we
have not incorporated into our model, one might expect to see this
pattern. Perhaps someone has done a comparative examination of this
across various domains or network types. Any users aware of this?

As for your other question about GWESP - yes, you are right that it does
not make sense for bipartite networks. GWDSP would make sense though,
and would capture an analogous type of process at the 4-cycle level, so
I ma glad to see that you include that. Without more knowledge of your
data, I don't have any advice for improving the geodesic fit. I'd
suggest perhaps trying ways to find other types of explicit or latent
clustering in your data. anyone else have any thoughts?

Thanks,
Steve
